events: Luther’s theses
The indulgence controversy begins. The next year Cajetan examines Luther at Augsburg.
Vitoria at Salamanca
Francisco de Vitoria takes the prime chair and lectures on the Summa of Thomas instead of the Sentences.
The Society of Jesus
Paul III approves the company of Ignatius of Loyola.
The Council of Trent
It meets in three periods until 1563. Laínez, Salmerón, Soto and Cano are among its theologians.
The Roman College
Ignatius opens the college that becomes the Gregorian University.
Molina’s Concordia
Printed at Lisbon. It reconciles grace and free will by God’s middle knowledge.
The congregation De auxiliis
Rome examines the quarrel of the Dominicans and the Jesuits over grace. In 1607 Paul V lets both schools teach.
Jansen’s Augustinus
Printed at Louvain two years after its author’s death.
Cum occasione
Innocent X condemns five propositions drawn from the Augustinus.
The Gallican Articles
The clergy of France limit the pope’s power. Bossuet writes their defense.
Unigenitus
Clement XI condemns 101 propositions of Pasquier Quesnel.
The Jesuits suppressed
Clement XIV dissolves the Society. Pius VII restores it in 1814.
The First Vatican Council
The primacy and infallibility of the pope are defined in 1870.
Aeterni Patris
Leo XIII calls the schools back to Thomas Aquinas.

III. Whether a material substance is something distinct from matter and form taken together, and their union.

disp.t: ON THE ESSENTIAL NATURE OF ACCIDENT IN GENERAL
secs: I. Whether accident in general signifies one concept or objective nature.
II. Whether the common definition of an accident consists in inherence.

disp.t: ON THE COMPARISON OF AN ACCIDENT TO SUBSTANCE
secs: I. Whether substance is prior in time to an accident.
II. Whether substance is prior in knowledge to an accident.

disp.t: ON THE DIVISION OF ACCIDENT INTO THE NINE HIGHEST GENERA
secs: I. Whether accident in common is immediately divided into quantity, quality, and the other highest genera of accidents.
II. Whether the division of accident into nine genera is sufficient.
III. ,. Whether the aforesaid division is univocal or analogical.

disp.t: ON CONTINUOUS QUANTITY
secs: I. What quantity is, especially continuous.
II. Whether the quantity of bulk is a thing distinct from material substance and its qualities.
III. Whether the essence of quantity consists in the reason of measure.
IV. Whether the formal concept and effect of continuous quantity is divisibility, or distinction, or the extension of the parts of the substance.
V. Whether in continuous quantity there are points, lines, and surfaces, which are true things, really distinct among themselves and from a body.
VI. Whether a line and a surface are proper species of continuous quantity, distinct from each other and from a body.
VII. Whether place is a true species of continuous quantity distinct from others.
VIII. Whether motion or its extension constitutes a proper species of continuous quantity.
IX. Whether time is per se a quantity constituting a peculiar species distinct from the rest.

disp.t: ON DISCRETE QUANTITY, AND THE COORDINATION OF THE CATEGORY OF QUANTITY, AND ITS PROPERTIES
secs: I. Whether discrete quantity is a proper species of quantity. Arguments for the negative side.
II. Whether discrete quantity is found in spiritual things.
III. Whether speech is a true species of quantity. Resolution.
IV. What the coordination of the genera and species of quantity is like.
V. What properties are attributed to quantity.

disp.t: On Quality, and Its Species in General
secs: I. What is the common ratio, or essential mode of quality
II. Whether quality is conveniently and sufficiently divided into four species
III. Whether all distinct species comprehend true and only qualities under themselves
IV. Whether the four species of quality are wholly distinct from one another
V. Whether the division of quality into four species is sufficient
VI. Whether the duplicated terms by which the said species are proposed signify their essential or accidental differences.
VII. What properties of qualities agree.

disp.t: On Potency and Act
secs: I. Whether potency is rightly and sufficiently divided into active and passive, and what each is.
II. Whether active and passive potency always differ really, or sometimes only by reason.
III. What is divided by that partition, and what its definition is.
IV. Exposition of the sense of the question.
V. Whether to each potency its proper act corresponds, and how.
VI. Whether the act is prior to potency in duration, perfection, definition and cognition.

disp.t: On Habits
secs: I. Whether habit exists, what it is, and in what subject habits are.
II. Whether habit is acquired in a potency moved according to place.
III. Whether there are habits in brutes.
IV. Whether there are proper habits in the intellect.
V. Whether a habit produces an act.
VI. What a habit effects in an act.
VII. Which acts a habit produces.
VIII. Whether acts are per se the efficient cause of habit.
IX. Whether a habit is made by one or by many acts.
X. Whether a habit is perfected by acts, and how
XI. What kind of extensive augmentation of a habit is, and what unity of habit corresponds to it.
XII. Whether and how habits are diminished and corrupted.
XIII. That there are genera and species of habits, and especially concerning the distinction of habits into practical and speculative.

disp.t: On the Contrariety of Qualities
secs: I. What opposition is, and how fourfold.
II. What is the proper definition of contraries, and the difference from other opposites.
III. Whether proper contrariety is found in all and only qualities.
IV. Whether contraries can in any way be together in the same subject.

disp.t: On the intension of qualities
secs: I. Whether an intensible and remissible quality is indivisible in itself, or composed of degrees of entity.
II. Whether the sole intensible quality is such, and why this does not suit all things.
III.
IV. Whether the intensive latitude of qualities has definite terms of intension and remission.

disp.t: On the real relation in general
secs: Whether relation is a true genus of real being, distinct from the others.
II. Whether a real categorical relation is distinguished really, or modally and by the nature of the thing, from substance, and from all absolute acci
III. How manifold relation is, and what is truly predicamental.
III. How many kinds of relation there are, and which is truly predicamental.
IV. How a predicamental respect differs from a transcendental one
V. What is the definition of a predicamental relation
VI. On the subject, the foundation and the terminus required for a predicamental relation
VII. On the foundation of the predicamental relation
VIII. On the term of predicamental relation
IX. What distinction is necessary between the foundation and the term
X. Whether the three genera of relations are rightly distinguished by Aristotle from a threefold foundation
XI. On the first kind of relations, founded in number or unity
XII. Concerning the second kind of relations founded in potency or action
XIII. A difficulty about the Philosopher's meaning is proposed
XIV. Whether the said division is sufficient and includes all relations
XV. Whether relations of the third genus are non-mutual, and in this differ from relations of the other genera
XVI. Whether the formal term of a relation is another relation, or some absolute reason
XVII. How a predicate "Ad aliquid" under a single supreme genus may be constituted through diverse subordinate genera and species even down to individ

disp.t: On action
secs: I. Whether action essentially denotes a relation to the principle of acting
II. Whether action essentially regards a term
III. Which respect, to the principle or to the term, is more essential to action, and whence it derives its specification
IV. Whether action, as action, states essentially a respect to the subject of inherence, and what that subject is
V. What finally is the nature of action, what its causes or properties
VI. What are the genera and species of actions, and how they are placed under one genus

disp.t: On Passion
secs: I. Whether passion in the thing itself differs from action
II. How passion is compared to motion or mutation, and what finally passion is
III. Whether actual inherence, or only aptitudinal inherence, is of the essence of passion
IV. Whether successive passion and momentary passion belong to the genus of passion, and how they differ under it

disp.t: On the Predicament When, as to the universe, about the durations of things
secs: I. Whether duration in a thing is distinct from the being of the thing that endures.
II. What is the formal nature of duration, and how, according to it, it is distinguished by reason from existence.
III. On eternity.
IV. Whether eternity include in its formal reason some respect of relation
V. What aevum is, and how it is distinguished from successive durations
VI. Whether aevum essentially differs from other permanent and created durations
VII. Whether permanent things, and those corruptible by their nature, have a proper and intrinsic duration, and what or what kind it is
VIII. Whether there is any proper duration of successive things, which is also successive, and is called time.
IX. Whether time in a thing is distinguished from motion.
X. First assertion.
XI. What things, and what this time measures in those same things
XII. What sort of duration pertains to the predicament When, and how such a predicament is to be constituted.

disp.t: Of Ubi
secs: I. Whether Ubi is something extrinsic or intrinsic to the body which is said to be somewhere, and what that thing is.
II. Whether the Where be the place of the body, so that by that alone it could truly be said to be in a place.
III. The meaning of the question is opened.
IV. What proportion the Ubi of body and spirit maintain between themselves.
V. Whether the Where (Ubi) belongs only to substances, or also to accidents.
VI. How the predicament Where is to be distinguished and ordered, and which properties are to be assigned to them.

disp.t: On Situs
secs: I. What situs is, and in what way it differs from Ubi.
Section 2. How situs and Ubi differ in concept.
II. What subjects, species, or properties may be attributed to this predicament.

disp.t: On Habit, as a Certain Kind of Accident
secs: I. Whether habit is something extrinsically denominating, and what that is.
II. What are the subjects, species, or properties of habitus.

disp.t: On the Beings of Reason
secs: I. Whether there is an ens rationis, and what essence it may have.
II. Whether a being of reason has a cause, and what that is.
III. Whether rational being is rightly divided into negation, privation, and relation.
IV. Whether the being of reason is sufficiently divided into negation, privation, and relation.
V. Negation and privation are compared, as they are in things.
VI. What is necessary for a relation of reason, and in how many ways it can be formed or conceived.

keys.say: The school of Thomas after Trent belonged to the Dominicans of Salamanca, Alcalá and Paris. The Carmelites wrote its great course.

names.bio: Founding master of the School of Salamanca, the Dominican who made Aquinas's Summa the classroom text in place of Lombard's Sentences and trained a generation of Spanish theologians. His relectiones on the Indians, war and civil and ecclesiastical power applied Thomist natural law to the Spanish empire and earned him the title father of international law. He published nothing himself. His students' transcriptions carried his method across Catholic Europe.

Vitoria's successor in the Salamanca chair, the emperor's theologian at Trent and a chief author of its decree on justification. His De natura et gratia, written at Trent, is the classic Dominican statement on nature, original sin and grace against Pelagian and Protestant readings. De iustitia et iure extends Thomist principles to economics, poverty and the rights of the conquered.

Francisco Zumel (Cumel), O. de M. (c. 1540–1607), Mercedarian professor of theology at Salamanca and provincial of his order for Castile. A figure of the Spanish Thomist revival, he defended Báñezian physical premotion against Molina in the De Auxiliis controversy. He is best known for his Commentaria on the First Part of the Summa.
